questions.q: What is the fastest way to define a name for a selected cell or range?
options: Type the name directly into the Name Box and press Enter
Change the cell's font color
Save the workbook as a new file
Press Ctrl+T to convert it to a Table
questions.explain: Typing a name into the Name Box (next to the formula bar) and pressing Enter is the fastest way to define a named range — Formulas → Define Name is the alternative when you need to set a specific scope.

questions.q: What is the real advantage of writing =B2*TaxRate instead of =B2*$B$1?
options: It's self-documenting — a reader can tell what the formula computes without checking what cell $B$1 holds
It calculates a different, more accurate result
It automatically converts the result to a percentage
It only works in Excel Online, not desktop Excel
questions.explain: Both formulas produce the same result — the named version is better because anyone reading it later understands what it means without cross-referencing another cell.

questions.q: Where can you view, edit, or delete every named range in a workbook at once?
options: The Name Manager (Formulas → Name Manager, or Ctrl+F3)
The Page Layout tab
The Print Preview screen
The Recycle Bin
questions.explain: The Name Manager lists every defined name in the workbook along with its value, what it refers to, and its scope, and lets you edit or delete any of them.

questions.q: What does a #REF! value next to a name in the Name Manager indicate?
options: Whatever that name used to point to was deleted, and formulas using that name are now broken
The name is spelled incorrectly
The name is currently in use by a formula, which is normal and expected
The workbook needs to be saved in a newer file format
questions.explain: #REF! next to a name means its underlying reference was deleted (e.g. the row or column it pointed to was removed) — every formula relying on that name is now broken until it's redefined.

questions.q: According to this lesson, does a Table (Lesson 3) create any entries in the Name Manager?
options: Yes — Excel automatically creates a name for a Table (like Table5) and it appears in the same Name Manager list
No — Tables and named ranges are completely unrelated features that never interact
Only if you manually rename the Table first
Only in Excel for Mac, not Windows
questions.explain: Every Table gets an automatic name (Table1, Table5, etc.) that shows up in the Name Manager alongside any names you define yourself.
